Langebaan fish farms

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A wave of anger rolls through Langebaan as fish farms look like they are here to stay

Unique Selling Point:
Beautiful lagoon, angry people, impacts on our audience, government wants to do the right thing but doing it badly already

Summary:
A red tide of anger has swept across the Langebaan Lagoon.

In 2014 Operation Phakisa, a government initiative to create jobs and investment announced an aquaculture or fish farming initiative in the greater Langebaan Lagoon. As usual the public participation process tried to ram what is now called the ADZ or aquaculture development zone through. But over 1000 residents and businesses objected to the lack of public participation and quickly formed themselves into the Save Langebaan lagoon action group. This grouping of residents, business owners, local fisherman, environmental lawyers, conservationists and scientists have raised a myriad of objections to the proposal.



Further information:
In short, the Department of forestry and fisheries in conjunction with Transnet port authorities have already, it seems, approved 7 potential lesees to farm mussels and alien finfish in several concessions inside the Saldahna Lagoon. These lesees are not small scale local fishermen, in fact the local fishermen are not really represented at all.

Our investigation of the directors of the companies advertised in April, even as the public participation process is still underway reveals that only one of the companies appears to be a small local fisherman. There are Chinese owned companies and at least two of the companies are linked to VIKING FISHING – a large industrial fishing company in Cape Town.


Solien Smit who represents small scale local fishermen, say they weren’t consulted at all and only found out about this in February this year. They have lodged objections during the public participation process.

So what is the problem? It may be easier to list them for this proposal
At least 4 kms of fish farms just off club Mykonos
There was an attempt to ram the EIA through without proper participation
The lagoon is a Ramsar listed site and already stressed. Aquaculture could send it over the edge
Water scientists show that the fish poo- called biofouling could destroy the water quality of the lagoon
Fish farming could destroy the tourism business which sustains the town
There are six kite surfing schools that bring in huge revenue – imagine kite surfers and yachts crashing into the fish cages. Its already happened in the pilot project
The ADZ will create 800 jobs, but potentially put another 3000 jobs in tourism at risk
Finfish farming need antibiotics and organophosphates to kill sea lice
These organophosphates kill seabirds
The cages break in storms and can become hazardous
The local people are not being empowered
Atlantic Salmon and Rainbow trout are alien species and could escape
Fish farms attract more sharks. To date there has never been a shark attack in Langebaan

The list goes on and on. Carte Blanche speaks to the scientists, the locals, the politicians, and the business men on both sides of the argument

Press Release:


Langebaan Lagoon
There is a storm brewing over the Langebaan Lagoon. Locals claim that an area of over 800 hectares, proposed for fish farming, will kill off a
flourishing and buoyant tourism economy that has created at least 3000 jobs in this west coast town. The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries
and Forestry disagrees, and they are pushing ahead with their plans. Locals say they are prepared to take their fight all the way to court, and
have organized themselves into an action group, determined to save the Langebaan lagoon. Carte Blanche investigates

Script:


Langebaan Final Script FOR TX Sunday 9th July 2017 FINAL

Commentary One 12 seconds
Every summer the beaches of Langebaan fill up with colour, as kite surfers and international water sports enthusiasts speed across the bay for the Langebaan downwind dash

Link
Langebaan has earned the reputation as the jewel of the Cape West Coast, attracting tourists from both here and across the world, now a wave of anger is washing through this famous lagoon

Commentary Two 20.5 seconds
884 hectares or, roughly 10% of Saldanha Bay is earmarked by government for an aquaculture development zone or ADZ, but locals fear fish farming will destroy the lagoon. And no lagoon means no tourism. Environmental lawyer Jennifer Kamerman

Jennifer Kamerman environmental lawyer
if it goes ahead Langebaan economy will collapse, we cannot see it as a sustainable development, and it will kill off a flourishing buoyant economy

Commentary Three 17seconds
To get an idea of how buoyant - Last year 287000 tourists visited the west coast national park. 3000 jobs in the town rely on tourism. Aquaculture has promised around 850 direct jobs, over ten years

Jennifer Kamerman
800 jobs being created over a ten 10 year period at best, is nothing to write home about. Hospitality industry and the eco tourism and the sport tourism industry here in Langebaan is booming, and thousands of jobs substantiated are at risk right now

Commentary Four 5.5 seconds
John Van der Vyver is spokesman for the Langebaan guild of kite surfing schools.

JOHN VAN DER VYFER
We have a pristine environment but we don’t have many economic possibilities, we are risking everything we have on the contingent outcome of this project and for me it’s like taking grocery money to the casino

Commentary five 7 seconds
Already in the recent storm, mussel rafts broke loose and floated across the bay onto the beaches

JOHN
When this stuff breaks free like in the storm, you hit one of those at 35 km’s per hour break your neck



Commentary six 27.5 seconds
Operation Phakisa has earmarked several industries across South Africa that can bring rapid economic development. There are already oyster and mussel farms in Saldanha, but Phakisa proposes much more. And 5000 tonnes per annum of salmon and rainbow trout in cages like these, will be phased in. But Langebaan Mayoral committee member for infrastructure and planning, Andre Kruger is concerned

Andre
Phakisa means hurry up. I support Phakisa but in this case, we can’t hurry up. We have to make the right decision to ensure we do not affect this whole area, killing the goose that’s laying the golden egg

Commentary seven 10.5 seconds
But at the Department of Agriculture, forestry and fisheries known as DAFF, they are pushing ahead. Andrea Bernatzeder is operations manager for aquaculture

Andrea
Most of what is planned is shellfish culture. Only 10% is finfish aquaculture, and shell fish has been done since 1980’s so it’s a well- established and feasible sector

Commentary eight 20 seconds
Realizing, no one was informed, a group of Langebaan volunteers scrambled to organise.
They challenged DAFF’S proposal, and canvassed the support of over 1000 businesses and residents. In May, Save Langebaan action group organized this beach protest. Clifford Wright is a founder volunteer

Clifford Wright
When they did the first public meeting they thought a few people would rock up. I think they have been surprised by the outcry. From our side, we will fight to the end

Commentary nine 12.5 seconds
DAFF environmental consultants SRK, say they have listened to concerns and already reduced the area by 50%, and point out there is no aquaculture planned in the lagoon itself.

Andrea
The size of the area can put people off but the more area we have the more area we have to play and move operations around

LINK
Where I am standing is more or less the start of Langebaan lagoon – in the distance is big bay and beyond that small bay – now because no aquaculture is planned for the lagoon itself doesn’t necessarily mean it’s going to be spared its impact




Andre Kruger
The ecology is such that it goes past the Industrial north and ends up in the marine protected area in the south, so if we do something wrong in the North it’s going to have an impact in the South.

Up sound Clifford and John

John
So this is the mouth of the lagoon its probably important to say that there is going to be no development here but this is your area of main concern
Definitely
John
What is proposed here?
Clifford Wright
Here you have your finfish salmon and trout – they have 42 hectares planned here and the balance of 367 hectares will be mussels and oysters. The main harbor is along here with port control coming out on this side. You’ve got the iron ore jetty- this is part of the ADZ development area along that side so this whole area is industry.
John
Two finfish farms over here not too much of a concern for you
Clifford
Its outside the bay and we feel it will be washed out
John
So it’s not an oversimplification to say what happens here and what happens here impacts here?
Clifford
Ya

Commentary ten 8.5 seconds
The area is only 10% of the bay says DAFF. But that’s the equivalent of 884 rugby fields
Says Clifford.

UP sound Clifford and John on boat
The farm starts from here to Paradise beach going along the beach with probably a kilometre buffer from the iron ore jetty and all the way back to the fish farms this side

Commentary eleven 19 seconds
Another criticism levelled by Save Langebaan Lagoon is that the public participation process was just a tick boxing exercise. But SRK say they have way exceeded those requirements. But the local fishermen, already marginalized, only found out about the process at the last minute

Solein Smit
There to my dismay did I realize that this was a project that was already well underway and we knew nothing about it and I could see the disappointment in the fishers that attended the meeting

John
This isn’t the first time that your members have been excluded from the fishing industry in general?

Solein Smit
We always have to fight to get anywhere and we don’t want to fight anymore we want to be included because we are born in Langebaan, we are traditional fishers and we want to be consulted

Commentary twelve 10.5 seconds
Copper, zinc, and manganese and over 50 thousand tonnes of iron ore leave this bay in 500 ships every year. But a lot more development is planned.

Up sound diving bubbles

10 .5 seconds
Already there are dead zones and and traces of heavy metals on the sea floor. This is a bay under pressure says local water specialist Christo Van Wijk.

John
How would you describe the marine ecosystem to the naked eye it looks quite healthy?
Christo
It’s not healthy, the whole ecosystem is under stress, and then you have all the impacts from the industry and all the land based human interactions as well.

Commentary thirteen 10 seconds
So Christo is perplexed, that the impact study done by DAFF’s environmental consultants SRK, is based on assumptions and rough estimates

Christo
The concern we have with the SRK study is its not site specific. If you look at aquaculture industry in the northern hemisphere, it’s deep waters so it’s a totally different scenario- we have in this closed system here, which is basically in Southern Africa, the major food source for endangered birds all over world into here and back, so it’s a very sensitive system and they are basing their information on desktop studies from elsewhere in the world

John
Isn’t a site- specific study, an obvious thing to do?
Christo
According to me yes, but it’s not done.

John to Andrea
One of the criticisms is that SRK has conducted a desk top study?
Andrea
Saldanha Bay is one of the most monitored and researched bay in South Africa, so In that respect it’s not necessary to do detailed studies

John
We have spoken to scientists who disagree
Andrea
We have done pilot studies we have seen that its feasible, and now our adoption is to do a precautionary approach in terms of scaling up

LINK
Now this is the pilot project for one of the potential lessees…There are six cages- each one holds around 18 000 salmon, but Save Langebaan Lagoon have been trying to get data on this study, but they say none has been forthcoming

Commentary fourteen 16seconds
These cages belong to Molopong, one of the lesees and a subsidiary of Viking Fishing
Tim Reddell is CEO of Viking. He says they have already invested R25 million rand on this project and given their data to DAFF

Tim Reddell
The thought process is that getting involved in aquaculture a is a quick way to make money is absolutely not the case
John
It seems to be the same old industry players – big companies that have been around for a long time is that a criticism that you are prepared to accept
Tim
Absolutely you will find us here 7 days a week. This is what we do for a living so to find us developing aquaculture would be the next logical step to move into

Commentary Fifteen 6.5 seconds
But it’s the excrement from 5000 tonnes of finfish that could really pollute the water

Christo
It’s basically Nitrogen and the debris that is coming from the fish that is excreted down to the bottom these things can eventually be dissolved in water column, and taken by current up to the lagoon, that is the concern

John
If this project goes ahead on the scale its planned what will this area look like in 5, 10, 15 years?
Christo
If it goes ahead we can have a Hartbeespoort scenario, it’s not a given, ……but we could
kill the bay close down the bay

Commentary sixteen 10 seconds
DAFF and Reddell say it will never get that bad. Aquaculture needs good quality water so they will monitor and reduce production as necessary




Tim
The water quality around the cages is checked every week, once a month the divers go down and check the benthos that is the underlying substrate so there are a number of checks and balances in place to ensure we co- exist and the minute we don’t co- exist our license would be revoked

Commentary seventeen 14.5 seconds
For now, the Basic Assessment report has been completed and it’s now up to Department of Environment to give the final go ahead, or not. DAFF believes the aquaculture can comfortably co- exist with, and even boost tourism

Andrea
So there is great tourism potential in terms of boat trips, tours to the farms, fresh product to the area, seafood festivals etc
John
Forgive me for smiling but that is not something I am quite getting – the tourism potential of a fish farm doesn’t make a huge amount of sense to me but maybe I am just being skeptical

Aquaculture is not really known in South Africa so there is a huge interest in terms of actually doing tours to the farms seeing how the farms operate, how do they harvest

Commentary eighteen 11.5 seconds
But there seems to be little common ground – SAVE LANGEBAAN LAGOON say there is no monitoring and compliance built into the projects, and many of their questions to DAFF remain unanswered.

Jennifer Kamerman
We are supported in law. Wer are going all the way with fighting this – the two are incongruent – we cannot have a flourishing langebaan community alongside the ADZ

THE END 12 00

PROMO ONE 10 seconds
A proposed new aquaculture development zone in Langebaan has many locals up in arms. They say it will destroy the flourishing tourism economy and pollute the lagoon.

PROMO TWO
Visitors from all over the world enjoy the water sports of Langebaan lagoon, but for how much longer
John
we are risking everything we have on the contingent outcome of this project and for me it’s like taking grocery money to the casino

PROMO THREE
Andrea
So there is great tourism potential in terms of boat trips, tours to the farms, fresh product to the area, seafood festivals etc
John
Forgive me for smiling but that is not something I am quite getting – the tourism potential of a fish farm doesn’t make a huge amount of sense to me

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A wave of anger rolls through Langebaan as fish farms look like they are here to stay
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Beautiful lagoon, angry people, impacts on our audience, government wants to do the right thing but doing it badly already
metadata.Summary: A red tide of anger has swept across the Langebaan Lagoon. In 2014 Operation Phakisa, a government initiative to create jobs and investment announced an aquaculture or fish farming initiative in the greater Langebaan Lagoon. As usual the public participation process tried to ram what is now called the ADZ or aquaculture development zone through. But over 1000 residents and businesses objected to the lack of public participation and quickly formed themselves into the Save Langebaan lagoon action group. This grouping of residents, business owners, local fisherman, environmental lawyers, conservationists and scientists have raised a myriad of objections to the proposal.
metadata.Further information: In short, the Department of forestry and fisheries in conjunction with Transnet port authorities have already, it seems, approved 7 potential lesees to farm mussels and alien finfish in several concessions inside the Saldahna Lagoon. These lesees are not small scale local fishermen, in fact the local fishermen are not really represented at all. Our investigation of the directors of the companies advertised in April, even as the public participation process is still underway reveals that only one of the companies appears to be a small local fisherman. There are Chinese owned companies and at least two of the companies are linked to VIKING FISHING – a large industrial fishing company in Cape Town. Solien Smit who represents small scale local fishermen, say they weren’t consulted at all and only found out about this in February this year. They have lodged objections during the public participation process. So what is the problem? It may be easier to list them for this proposal At least 4 kms of fish farms just off club Mykonos There was an attempt to ram the EIA through without proper participation The lagoon is a Ramsar listed site and already stressed. Aquaculture could send it over the edge Water scientists show that the fish poo- called biofouling could destroy the water quality of the lagoon Fish farming could destroy the tourism business which sustains the town There are six kite surfing schools that bring in huge revenue – imagine kite surfers and yachts crashing into the fish cages. Its already happened in the pilot project The ADZ will create 800 jobs, but potentially put another 3000 jobs in tourism at risk Finfish farming need antibiotics and organophosphates to kill sea lice These organophosphates kill seabirds The cages break in storms and can become hazardous The local people are not being empowered Atlantic Salmon and Rainbow trout are alien species and could escape Fish farms attract more sharks. To date there has never been a shark attack in Langebaan The list goes on and on. Carte Blanche speaks to the scientists, the locals, the politicians, and the business men on both sides of the argument
